CAIL Relay: Data Simulation, Exploratory Analysis and Anomaly Detection¶

Catalyst 2026 · Case Study Challenge #5 · Team #24
Challenge sponsor CAIL Systems Inc.
Challenge Managing Mission Critical Systems with AI
Team Adan Abdullahi (Build: data + AI) · Rong Hao (UX design) · Dhruva Rau (Business case + content)
Date October 17, 2026

Problem statement¶

"How might we use AI to help the next generation of IT operators understand, monitor, and troubleshoot mission-critical enterprise systems through natural language, while preserving the expertise of experienced professionals?"

Purpose of this notebook¶

CAIL's systems (HPE NonStop) run banking, payments and telecom transactions 24/7. The case does not provide real system data, and its rules forbid access to production systems or customer data. This notebook therefore:

  1. Generates 24 hours of realistic, simulated HPE NonStop operational data with three planted incidents
  2. Explores the data (structure, quality, distributions, relationships)
  3. Detects the incidents with unsupervised anomaly detection, without telling the model where they are
  4. Evaluates detection against the known incidents
  5. Exports the data that the CAIL Relay AI assistant reads

Where this fits¶

Banks already run monitoring tools on HPE NonStop (ASAP, Prognosis, ViewSys) that detect problems and rank them by severity. CAIL Relay does not replace them: it reads their alerts, explains them in plain English, suggests the next safe command, and preserves expert knowledge, inside CAIL's terminal. Because we cannot access those tools, our anomaly detection simulates the alerts they would raise, and doubles as a fallback for systems without one.

Note: all data is simulated. Names follow real NonStop conventions ($PAY1, $DATA01, TMF, EMS). Command syntax is illustrative.

2. Data generation¶

Runs simulate_nonstop.py, which:

  • builds a normal day (busier at midday, quieter at night, small random noise; fixed seed = repeatable)
  • plants three incidents at known times
  • writes EMS-style alerts and a command catalog with risk labels
  • runs anomaly detection (rolling z-score + Isolation Forest + trend check)
  • exports everything to data/

Key findings: relationships

  • CPU load and TPS move together in normal operation (more transactions, more CPU work)
  • Response time rises with CPU 1 load and with TMF backouts (correlation ~0.6 to 0.7): overloaded CPUs slow customers down
  • Problems in one component show up in others. This is CAIL's "interconnected risks" point, and why the AI must read several metrics together, not one at a time

def zoom(start, end, cols, title):
    w = m[(m.t >= start) & (m.t <= end)]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(len(cols), 1, figsize=(12, max(2.6, 1.9*len(cols))), sharex=True, squeeze=False)
    ax = ax[:, 0]
    for a, (c, col) in zip(ax, cols):
        a.plot(w.t, w[c], color=col); a.set_ylabel(c, fontsize=8)
        a.scatter(w.t[w.anomaly], w[c][w.anomaly], color=RED, s=10, zorder=3)
    ax[-1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%H:%M"))
    ax[0].set_title(title + "  (red dots = minutes flagged by ML)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Key findings: INC-001

  • At 02:14, CPU 2 jumps from ~28% to ~96-99%; TPS falls from ~480 to 168-210
  • The $PAY1 queue grows by ~165 messages per minute, reaching ~1,800; $PAY1 stops doing I/O (last I/O climbs to minutes)
  • Signature = one CPU maxed + queue growing + no I/O = a looping process, not a capacity problem
  • After the 02:24 SWITCH to the backup, CPU 3 takes the load and everything returns to normal by ~02:34
  • Detected at 02:14, the same minute it started

INC-002 · 14:30 · CPU 3 hardware failure (CAIL's scenario)¶

In [14]:
zoom("2026-10-17 14:15", "2026-10-17 15:20",
     [("cpu3_pct", TEAL), ("cpu1_pct", GREY), ("response_ms", RED), ("tmf_backout_pct", ORANGE)],
     "INC-002: CPU 3 down")

Key findings: INC-002

  • CPU 3 drops to 0%; its process pairs take over on CPU 1, which jumps to ~97%
  • Response time more than doubles (to ~138 ms) and TMF backouts rise to ~2.3% (vs ~0.2%)
  • The system keeps running (fault tolerance works) but with less capacity. Exactly CAIL's story: the hardware failed, the remaining CPUs absorb the load, and an operator must notice and act
  • Detected at 14:30, the same minute as the CPU failure

Key findings: events

  • 21 events: 12 INFO, 8 WARN, 1 CRIT
  • Each incident produces a short chain of alerts across several subsystems (CPU, TMF, Pathway, Disk). A junior must connect them; the AI does this automatically
  • Each alert carries the monitoring tool that would raise it (ASAP, Prognosis, ViewSys or EMS) and a severity rank (1 = most urgent), matching how those tools prioritise problems
  • The audit trail ("senior sign-off requested", "approved by R. Diaz") shows the human-in-the-loop flow CAIL requires

9. Anomaly detection¶

Three unsupervised detectors. None is told when the incidents happen. In production, tools like ASAP or Prognosis provide this detection; ours simulates it so the AI has realistic alerts to work with.

Method Type How it works Good at
Rolling z-score Statistics Compares each minute to the previous 60 minutes. Flags if more than 4 standard deviations away Sudden jumps in one metric
Isolation Forest Unsupervised ML Randomly splits the data; unusual points get isolated in fewer splits Unusual combinations across metrics
Trend check Statistics Disk growth rate over the last 15 minutes vs normal (~0.002%/min) Slow drift that z-score misses

Why three? Our first version used only z-score + Isolation Forest and reached only 57% recall: it caught the two sudden faults perfectly but only 44% of the slow disk fault, because a rolling z-score's baseline drifts along with a slow change. Adding the trend check raised recall to 90% with no extra false alarms.

A minute is flagged if any detector flags it. No labels and no training data needed: the model learns "normal" from the day itself.

9.0 Workflow: preprocessing, training and testing¶

Unsupervised learning follows the same overall steps as supervised learning, with one difference: we train on normal data only, without labels.

Step Supervised (e.g. loan default) This project (unsupervised)
1. EDA Explore features and label Sections 3 to 8
2. Preprocess Clean, encode, scale Quality checks (section 4) + standardise each metric with the training day's mean and std
3. Split Train/test split of labelled rows Training day = a separate clean normal day (Oct 16). Test day = the incident day (Oct 17)
4. Train Learn the label Isolation Forest learns what normal looks like from the training day
5. Threshold Usually 0.5 probability Top 0.5% of training-day scores = the limit for "unusual"
6. Test Predict on test set Score every minute of the unseen test day
7. Evaluate vs labels vs the known incidents (section 10)

The z-score and trend check are rules, so they need no training; they use a rolling 60-minute and 15-minute window.

ax.set_xlabel("Isolation Forest score (higher = more unusual)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Train on normal, test on unseen day: incidents land right of the threshold"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Training day: 2026-10-16 | rows: 1440 | incidents: 0
Test day:     2026-10-17 | rows: 1440 | incidents: 3
Isolation Forest threshold (99.5th percentile of training scores): 0.548

Key findings: training and testing

  • The model never saw the incidents during training: it learned only from a clean normal day
  • Normal minutes from both days score low and overlap; incident minutes score much higher and fall past the threshold
  • This is the honest, out-of-sample test: results in section 10 reflect performance on new data

10. Evaluation against ground truth¶

In [21]:
def scores(pred):
    tp = int((pred & gt).sum()); fp = int((pred & ~gt).sum()); fn = int((~pred & gt).sum()); tn = int((~pred & ~gt).sum())
    prec = tp / max(tp + fp, 1); rec = tp / max(tp + fn, 1)
    return {"flagged_minutes": int(pred.sum()), "TP": tp, "FP": fp, "FN": fn, "TN": tn,
            "accuracy": round((tp + tn) / len(pred), 3), "precision": round(prec, 3),
            "recall": round(rec, 3), "F1": round(2 * prec * rec / max(prec + rec, 1e-9), 3)}
evaluation = pd.DataFrame({"z-score": scores(m.z_anomaly), "Isolation Forest": scores(m.iso_anomaly),
                           "Trend check": scores(m.trend_anomaly), "Combined": scores(m.anomaly)}).T

10.1 Confusion matrix (combined detector, per minute)¶

In [22]:
tp = int((m.anomaly & gt).sum()); fp = int((m.anomaly & ~gt).sum())
fn = int((~m.anomaly & gt).sum()); tn = int((~m.anomaly & ~gt).sum())
cmx = np.array([[tn, fp], [fn, tp]])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 3.6))
ax.imshow(cmx, cmap="Blues"); ax.grid(False)
for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(cmx):
    ax.text(j, i, f"{v}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, color="white" if v > 600 else "black")
ax.set_xticks([0, 1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["Predicted normal", "Predicted anomaly"])
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels(["Actual normal", "Actual incident"])
ax.set_title("Confusion matrix"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

How to read it

  • TN (top-left): normal minutes correctly left alone
  • FP (top-right): false-alarm minutes. Only 7, all isolated single minutes, and none became an alert (an alert needs 3+ minutes in a row)
  • FN (bottom-left): incident minutes not flagged, mostly the last recovery minutes when metrics are already back near normal
  • TP (bottom-right): incident minutes correctly flagged

Why accuracy alone is misleading: 88% of minutes are normal, so a model that never raises an alarm would still score ~88% accuracy and catch nothing. That is why precision, recall and F1 matter more for anomaly detection.

Key findings: detection performance

  • Incident level: 3 of 3 incidents detected (100% recall), and 3 of 3 alert windows were real incidents (100% precision)
  • Minute level (combined, tested on an unseen day): accuracy ~99%, precision ~96%, recall ~93%, F1 ~0.94
  • 7 false-alarm minutes in 24 hours, all isolated blips; none became an operator alert, so operators see 3 alerts, all real
  • Each detector covers a different fault type: z-score = sudden spikes, Isolation Forest = unusual combinations, trend check = slow drift. Alone each recalls 17-58%; combined, 90%
  • Model iteration: v1 (z-score + Isolation Forest, same-day) had 57% recall; v2 added the trend check for slow drift (90%); v3 trains Isolation Forest on a separate normal day and tests on the incident day (93% recall, the honest out-of-sample result)
  • Lead time: INC-001 and INC-002 detected the same minute they started; INC-003 detected 40 minutes before the first EMS alert

Key findings: safety by design

  • 9 commands: 7 SAFE (read-only), 1 CAUTION, 1 HIGH RISK
  • The AI can only suggest commands from this list, each with a risk label and a source to cite
  • HIGH RISK commands require senior sign-off: this meets CAIL's Human Oversight and Explainable AI requirements

12. Summary of key findings¶

# Finding Why it matters for CAIL
1 24h of clean, realistic NonStop data with 3 planted incidents, including CAIL's CPU-failure scenario Lets us demo safely without production access (case requirement)
2 Each incident has a distinct multi-metric signature The AI must read metrics together, like a senior does
3 Unsupervised detection, tested on an unseen day, found 3 of 3 incidents: ~96% precision, ~93% recall, F1 0.94, zero false alerts Early, trustworthy alerts without labelled data
4 Disk issue detected 40 minutes before the first system alert Earlier action, less downtime risk
5 A command catalog with risk labels and sources constrains the AI Safe, explainable, human-approved recommendations

13. How this feeds CAIL Relay¶

metrics + events  ─►  anomaly detection  ─►  anomalies
        │                                       │
        └──────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
  system prompt + command catalog + runbooks  ─►  LLM  ─►  plain-English answer
                                                          + suggested command
                                                          + risk + why + source
                                                          ─►  operator approves

ML finds the problem. The LLM explains it and suggests the next safe step. The human decides.

14. Assumptions and limitations¶

  • All data is simulated; real NonStop metrics would be noisier and need tuning (thresholds, window sizes, contamination rate)
  • Command names follow NonStop conventions but syntax is illustrative and must be verified against HPE manuals
  • Isolation Forest is trained on one simulated normal day; in production it would be trained on weeks of real normal history and retrained regularly
  • Ground truth is known only because we planted the incidents
